claim: U2OS cells do not express ATRX, a known contributing factor to HR.
source: U2OS cells have been widely used as a model cell line for DNA repair studies, however, it is important to note that U2OS cells do not express ATRX, a known contributing factor to HR (Elbakry et al., 2021; Juhász et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Elbakry et al., 2021; Juhász et al., 2018).

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 and homology-directed repair were used to insert a 3x-FLAG-HaloTag at endogenous genomic loci in U2OS cells.
source: To investigate the dynamics of DNA repair proteins at the single-molecule level in living cells, we used CRISPR-Cas9 and homology-directed repair to insert a 3x-FLAG-HaloTag at their endogenous genomic loci in U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: All cell lines were homozygously edited except for Halo-SHLD2 which had one tagged allele and a frameshift mutation in the second allele.
source: All cell lines were homozygously edited except for Halo-SHLD2 which had one tagged allele and a frameshift mutation in the second allele (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and E, and Sanger sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HaloTagged proteins were expressed at or near endogenous protein levels.
source: HaloTagged proteins validated by Western blotting were expressed at or near endogenous protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: NBS1, MDC1, 53BP1, RIF1, RNF168, RNF169, and DNA-PKcs localized to the nucleus.
source: As previously described, NBS1, MDC1, 53BP1, RIF1, RNF168, RNF169, and DNA-PKcs localized to the nucleus, whereas SHLD3, SHLD2, SHLD1, and REV7 were found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus (Figure 2A), suggesting that the HaloTag may not impact the proper cellular localization of these proteins (Noordermeer et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies (Noordermeer et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2016).

claim: SHLD3, SHLD2, SHLD1, and REV7 were found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus.
source: As previously described, NBS1, MDC1, 53BP1, RIF1, RNF168, RNF169, and DNA-PKcs localized to the nucleus, whereas SHLD3, SHLD2, SHLD1, and REV7 were found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus (Figure 2A), suggesting that the HaloTag may not impact the proper cellular localization of these proteins (Noordermeer et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies (Noordermeer et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2016).

claim: All HaloTagged proteins except ATM and DNA-PKcs showed dramatic increases in DNA damage induced foci formation after Zeocin treatment.
source: While very few foci were detected in the absence of DNA damage in any of the cell lines, we observed dramatic increases in DNA damage induced foci formation for all proteins except for ATM and DNA-PKcs which would not be expected due to the limited number of these proteins that localize to DSBs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Halo-ATM, Halo-MDC1, Halo-53BP1, and Halo-SHLD2 cell lines were more sensitive to Zeocin than control cells.
source: Four cell lines were more sensitive to Zeocin than control cells including Halo-ATM, Halo-MDC1, Halo-53BP1, and Halo-SHLD2.
evidence: The claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The HaloTag-ATM cell line was as sensitive to Zeocin as U2OS cells treated with the ATM inhibitor (ATMi) (KU-55933).
source: The HaloTag-ATM cell line was as sensitive to Zeocin as U2OS cells treated with the ATM inhibitor (ATMi) (KU-55933), which could not be alleviated by moving the HaloTag to the C-terminus of ATM, demonstrating that HaloTagging ATM at either end results in a non-functional protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: HaloTagging ATM at either end results in a non-functional protein.
source: The HaloTag-ATM cell line was as sensitive to Zeocin as U2OS cells treated with the ATM inhibitor (ATMi) (KU-55933), which could not be alleviated by moving the HaloTag to the C-terminus of ATM, demonstrating that HaloTagging ATM at either end results in a non-functional protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: The Halo-53BP1 and Halo-MDC1 cell lines had modestly increased sensitivity to Zeocin but were significantly more resistant than their knockout counterparts.
source: The Halo-53BP1 and Halo-MDC1 cell lines had modestly increased sensitivity to Zeocin but were significantly more resistant than their knockout counterparts, demonstrating they are partially functional (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by clonogenic survival assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Halo-53BP1 and Halo-MDC1 are partially functional.
source: The Halo-53BP1 and Halo-MDC1 cell lines had modestly increased sensitivity to Zeocin but were significantly more resistant than their knockout counterparts, demonstrating they are partially functional (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of Zeocin sensitivity between HaloTagged and knockout cell lines.

claim: Absolute protein abundance of HaloTagged proteins in U2OS cells ranged from ~1600 (ATM) to 180,000 (REV7) molecules per cell.
source: After correcting for differences in fluorescence intensity cause by SDS-PAGE migration patterns, HaloTagged protein abundance ranged from ~1600 (ATM) – 180,000 (REV7) molecules per cell (Table 1), with ATM (~1600–4200 molecules per cell), SHLD1 (~7300–8100 molecules per cell), SHLD2 (~7300 molecules per cell), and SHLD3 (~4000–5600 molecules per cell) clones having the lowest expression level (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence quantification data presented in Table 1.

claim: ATM, SHLD1, SHLD2, and SHLD3 clones had the lowest expression levels.
source: After correcting for differences in fluorescence intensity cause by SDS-PAGE migration patterns, HaloTagged protein abundance ranged from ~1600 (ATM) – 180,000 (REV7) molecules per cell (Table 1), with ATM (~1600–4200 molecules per cell), SHLD1 (~7300–8100 molecules per cell), SHLD2 (~7300 molecules per cell), and SHLD3 (~4000–5600 molecules per cell) clones having the lowest expression level (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence quantification data presented in Table 1.

claim: DNA-PKcs and NBS1 accumulated rapidly after laser microirradiation, with t1/2 = 22.1 s and t1/2 = 31.3 s, respectively.
source: DNA-PKcs and NBS1 accumulated rapidly after LMI, with a t1/2 = 22.1 s and t1/2 = 31.3 s, respectively, consistent with their known roles in the early steps of the DNA damage response (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MDC1 (t1/2 = 76.5 s) and RNF168 (t1/2 = 69.4 s) arrived at similar times.
source: MDC1 (t1/2 = 76.5 s) and RNF168 (t1/2 = 69.4 s) arrived at similar times, consistent with rapid ubiquitin deposition at DSBs dependent upon MDC1 mediated RNF8 and RNF168 recruitment (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNF169 (t1/2 = 185.8 s) was significantly delayed compared to RNF168.
source: RNF169 (t1/2 = 185.8 s) was significantly delayed compared to RNF168 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that RNF169 requires chromatin modification by RNF168 prior to its recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNF169 requires chromatin modification by RNF168 prior to its recruitment.
source: RNF169 (t1/2 = 185.8 s) was significantly delayed compared to RNF168 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that RNF169 requires chromatin modification by RNF168 prior to its recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the delayed recruitment kinetics of RNF169 compared to RNF168.

claim: 53BP1 and RIF1 both accumulated slowly at LMI sites with comparable kinetics (t1/2 = 669.0 s, t1/2 = 550.8 s, respectively).
source: 53BP1 and RIF1 both accumulated slowly at LMI sites with comparable kinetics (t1/2 = 669.0 s, t1/2 = 550.8 s, respectively) (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of SHLD3 completely eliminated SHLD2 foci-formation after Zeocin treatment.
source: While SHLD3 wildtype cells supported SHLD2 foci-formation after Zeocin treatment, loss of SHLD3 completely eliminated SHLD2 foci-formation, consistent with the well-known genetic dependency of SHLD2 on SHLD3 and with the hypothesis that at the time SHLD2 accumulation begins sufficient SHLD3 is present at DNA breaks to initiate SHLD2 recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Halo-SHLD2 and Halo-SHLD3 were simultaneously recruited to DNA lesions in comparable amounts.
source: In these experiments Halo-SHLD2 and Halo-SHLD3 were simultaneously recruited to DNA lesions in comparable amounts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After Halo-SHLD2 accumulation plateaued, Halo-SHLD3 continued to accumulate in excess of Halo-SHLD2.
source: After Halo-SHLD2 accumulation plateaued, Halo-SHLD3 continued to accumulate in excess of Halo-SHLD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser microirradiation recruitment kinetics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for freely moving particles ranged from Dfree = 1.0–3.7 μm2/s.
source: The diffusion coefficient for freely moving particles ranged from Dfree = 1.0–3.7 μm2/s, which are all lower than the diffusion coefficient measured for the HaloTag-3XNLS (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The diffusion coefficients measured for SHLD1 (Dfree = 3.7), SHLD2 (Dfree = 1.8), and SHLD3 (Dfree = 2.3) were significantly different from each other.
source: The diffusion coefficients measured for SHLD1 (Dfree = 3.7), SHLD2 (Dfree = 1.8), and SHLD3 (Dfree = 2.3) were significantly different from each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The shieldin complex is not preassembled in the nucleoplasm.
source: This suggests that the shieldin complex is not preassembled in the nucleoplasm, which is consistent with the distinct recruitment kinetics to LMI induced sites of DNA damage we observed for the shieldin complex components (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the significantly different diffusion coefficients of SHLD1, SHLD2, and SHLD3.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for bound particles in unperturbed cells ranged from Dbound = 0.02–0.10 μm2/s.
source: The diffusion coefficient for bound particles in unperturbed cells ranged from Dbound = 0.02–0.10 μm2/s, which are all faster than Halo-H2B (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Halo-H2B had a Dbound of 0.012 μm2/s, while the diffusion coefficient for bound MDC1 molecules was two-fold higher (Dbound = 0.024 μm2/s).
source: Consistent with this expectation, Halo-H2B had a Dbound of 0.012 μm2/s, while the diffusion coefficient for bound MDC1 molecules was two-fold higher (Dbound = 0.024 μm2/s).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 53BP1 had the fastest diffusing bound particles (Dbound = 0.099 μm2/s).
source: On the other hand, 53BP1 which can diffuse within phase-separated compartments had the fastest diffusing bound particles (Dbound = 0.099 μm2/s).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A wide range of the fraction of molecules bound to chromatin (Fbound = 23–69%) was observed in unperturbed cells.
source: We observed a wide range of the fraction of molecules bound to chromatin (Fbound = 23–69%) in unperturbed cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The chromatin bound fraction of MDC1 (Fbound = 69%) and RIF1 (Fbound = 68%) in unperturbed cells was comparable to that of HaloTag-H2B (Fbound = 66%).
source: Strikingly, the chromatin bound fraction of MDC1 (Fbound = 69%) and RIF1 (Fbound = 68%) in unperturbed cells was comparable to that of HaloTag-H2B (Fbound = 66%), suggesting that these DNA repair factors are constitutively associated with chromatin and may search for DNA breaks by local chromatin scanning (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MDC1 and RIF1 are constitutively associated with chromatin and may search for DNA breaks by local chromatin scanning.
source: Strikingly, the chromatin bound fraction of MDC1 (Fbound = 69%) and RIF1 (Fbound = 68%) in unperturbed cells was comparable to that of HaloTag-H2B (Fbound = 66%), suggesting that these DNA repair factors are constitutively associated with chromatin and may search for DNA breaks by local chromatin scanning (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high chromatin bound fraction of MDC1 and RIF1 in unperturbed cells.

claim: After Zeocin treatment, a significant increase in the fraction of static particles was observed for RNF169, 53BP1, SHLD2, SHLD3, and DNA-PKcs.
source: After Zeocin treatment, we observed a significant increase in the fraction of static particles for RNF169, 53BP1, SHLD2, SHLD3, and DNA-PKcs (Figure 5D), consistent with their recruitment to DNA breaks.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Within DNA repair foci 29% of 53BP1 molecules moved with a slow diffusion coefficient (Dfree2=0.6 µm2/s) compared to 17% of 53BP1 trajectories that did not overlap with DNA repair foci.
source: Within DNA repair foci 29% of 53BP1 molecules moved with a slow diffusion coefficient (Dfree2=0.6 µm2/s) compared to 17% of 53BP1 trajectories that did not overlap with DNA repair foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The fluorescence half-life of Halo-H2B was 7.7 seconds under imaging conditions.
source: The fluorescence half-life of Halo-H2B was 7.7 seconds under our imaging conditions (Figure 6B), which sets the upper limit for our residence time analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by residence time analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All DNA repair factors analyzed dissociated from chromatin more rapidly than histone H2B with half-lives ranging from t1/2 = 2.4 seconds for Halo-53BP1 to t1/2 = 5.8 s for Halo-MDC1.
source: All DNA repair factors analyzed dissociated from chromatin more rapidly than histone H2B with half-lives ranging from t1/2 = 2.4 seconds for Halo-53BP1 to t1/2 = 5.8 s for Halo-MDC1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by residence time analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The induction of DNA damage using zeocin increased the residence time of Halo-53BP (t1/2 ZEO = 3.6 s), Halo-SHLD2 (t1/2 ZEO = 4.9 s), and Halo-SHLD3 (t1/2 ZEO = 5.8 s).
source: The induction of DNA damage using zeocin increased to residence time of Halo-53BP (t1/2 ZEO = 3.6 s), Halo-SHLD2 (t1/2 ZEO = 4.9 s), and Halo-SHLD3 (t1/2 ZEO = 5.8 s) (Figure 6C), consistent with the increase in the chromatin bound fraction of these proteins observed in our Spot-On analysis (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by residence time analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WT MDC1, and MDC1 ΔPST formed foci after zeocin treatment, while MDC1 ΔBRCT was not recruited to DNA damage induced foci.
source: WT MDC1, and MDC1 ΔPST formed foci after zeocin treatment, while MDC1 ΔBRCT was not recruited to DNA damage induced foci (Figure 7C), consistent with previous observations that BRCT-γH2AX binding is essential for MDC1 foci formation and does not require the PST domain (Stucki et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7C and citation to a previous study (Stucki et al., 2005).

claim: The BRCT domains of MDC1 are the primary driver of MDC1 recruitment to DNA lesions.
source: This suggests that the BRCT domains of MDC1 are the primary driver of MDC1 recruitment to DNA lesions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MDC1 ΔBRCT was not recruited to DNA damage induced foci.

claim: Deletion of the BRCT domains did not alter the diffusion behavior of MDC1.
source: WT MDC1 transiently expressed in ΔMDC1 behaved identically to endogenously tagged MDC1 (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 5B–C), and deletion of the BRCT domains did not alter the diffusion behavior of MDC1 (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Deletion of the PST repeat domain almost completely eliminated the fraction of MDC1 molecules associated with chromatin.
source: In contrast, deletion of the PST repeat domain almost completely eliminated the fraction of MDC1 molecules associated with chromatin (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The PST repeat domain of MDC1 mediates the constitutive chromatin association of MDC1 even in the absence of DNA damage.
source: This suggests that the PST repeat domain of MDC1 mediates the constitutive chromatin association of MDC1 even in the absence of DNA damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of the PST repeat domain almost completely eliminated the fraction of MDC1 molecules associated with chromatin.

claim: Upon deletion of the PST repeat region, a significant increase in chromatin-bound MDC1 was observed after Zeocin exposure.
source: In contrast, upon deletion of the PST repeat region, we observed a significant increase in chromatin-bound MDC1 after Zeocin exposure (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of HaloTagged WT MDC1 led to a significantly higher number of GFP positive cells compared to MDC1 knockout cells.
source: Expression of HaloTagged WT MDC1 led to a significantly higher number of GFP positive cells compared to MDC1 knockout cells, consistent with HaloTagged MDC1 being capable of supporting HR (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by DR-GFP assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HR efficiency was significantly reduced to a similar degree when MDC1 lacking the PST- or BRCT-domains was expressed.
source: In contrast, HR efficiency was significantly reduced to a similar degree when MDC1 lacking the PST- or BRCT-domains was expressed, which was previously documented by others (Xie et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by DR-GFP assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and citation to a previous study (Xie et al., 2007).

claim: HaloTagged WT and ΔPST MDC1 were sufficient to promote recruitment of 53BP1 to DSB sites, while 53BP1 recruitment was defective in ΔMDC1 cells or cells expressing MDC1 lacking the BRCT domain.
source: Additionally, HaloTagged WT and ΔPST MDC1 were sufficient to promote recruitment of 53BP1 to DSB sites, while 53BP1 recruitment was defective in ΔMDC1 cells or cells expressing MDC1 lacking the BRCT domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both the PST- and BRCT-domains are critical for efficient HR while the PST domain is not required for 53BP1 recruitment to DSBs.
source: Importantly, both the PST- and BRCT-domains are critical for efficient HR while the PST domain is not required for 53BP1 recruitment to DSBs, suggesting that while MDC1-chromatin binding is important for HR, this interaction may be dispensable for 53BP1-dependent DNA end-joining.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the DR-GFP assay and immunofluorescence data.

claim: MDC1 is constitutively tethered to chromatin by its PST repeat region and is enriched at DNA lesions via the interaction of the BRCT domains with γH2AX.
source: Taken together, these observations support a model in which MDC1 is constitutively tethered to chromatin by its PST repeat region and is enriched at DNA lesions via the interaction of the BRCT domains with γH2AX.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of live-cell single-molecule imaging, DR-GFP assay, and immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: Repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) is integral to preserving genomic integrity.
source: Repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) is integral to preserving genomic integrity.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in the field of DNA repair.

claim: In mammalian cells two main pathways exist for resolving DNA DSBs, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination repair (HR).
source: In mammalian cells two main pathways exist for resolving DNA DSBs, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination repair (HR) (Scully et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Scully et al., 2019).

claim: HR requires a sister chromatid to serve as a template for high-fidelity DSB repair and is limited to S- and G2-phases of the cell cycle.
source: HR requires a sister chromatid to serve as a template for high-fidelity DSB repair and is limited to S- and G2-phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in the field of DNA repair.

claim: NHEJ functions independently of a repair template by ligating together broken DNA ends often leading to genomic insertions and deletions.
source: In contrast, NHEJ functions independently of a repair template by ligating together broken DNA ends often leading to genomic insertions and deletions.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in the field of DNA repair.

claim: NHEJ functions ubiquitously throughout G1-, S-, and G2-phases of the cell cycle.
source: Because of the toxicity of persistent, unrepaired DNA DSBs, NHEJ functions ubiquitously throughout G1-, S-, and G2-phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in the field of DNA repair.

claim: NHEJ-dependent repair represents the main pathway resolving the bulk of DSBs arising in human cells.
source: While cells balance the use of NHEJ and HR particularly in S- and G2-phase, NHEJ-dependent repair represents the main pathway resolving the bulk of DSBs arising in human cells either through rapid recruitment of the core NHEJ complex (DNA-PKcs, KU70, KU80, XLF, XRCC4, and LIG4) at unresected DNA ends or after 53BP1-Shieldin mediated end fill-in of previously resected DSBs (Setiaputra and Durocher, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Setiaputra and Durocher, 2019).

claim: DSB detection can be carried out both by the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer to directly recruit DNA-PKcs as well as ATM kinase and the MRN (Mre11, Rad50, and NBS1) complex which associate with DNA breaks leading to phosphorylation of H2AX at S139 (γH2AX) by ATM.
source: DSB detection can be carried out both by the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer to directly recruit DNA-PKcs as well as ATM kinase and the MRN (Mre11, Rad50, and NBS1) complex which associate with DNA breaks leading to phosphorylation of H2AX at S139 (γH2AX) by ATM (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).

claim: DDR signal amplification is mediated by MDC1, RNF8, and RNF168.
source: Next, DDR signal amplification is mediated by MDC1, RNF8, and RNF168 (Doil et al., 2009; Kolas et al., 2007; Lukas et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Doil et al., 2009; Kolas et al., 2007; Lukas et al., 2004).

claim: MDC1 directly binds γH2AX through its C-terminal BRCT domains leading to recruitment of RNF8 and K63-linked polyubiquitylation of linker histone H1.
source: MDC1 directly binds γH2AX through its C-terminal BRCT domains leading to recruitment of RNF8 and K63-linked polyubiquitylation of linker histone H1 (Mailand et al., 2007; Thorslund et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Mailand et al., 2007; Thorslund et al., 2015).

claim: K63-linked ubiquitination serves as a docking site for RNF168 which further amplifies the DDR signal via its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity by depositing monoubiquitin marks onto H2A at K13 and K15 (H2AK13ubK15ub).
source: K63-linked ubiquitination serves as a docking site for RNF168 which further amplifies the DDR signal via its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity by depositing monoubiquitin marks onto H2A at K13 and K15 (H2AK13ubK15ub) (Mattiroli et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Mattiroli et al., 2012).

claim: RNF169 binds H2AK13ubK15ub deposited by RNF168.
source: One key regulator of this choice is RNF169 which binds H2AK13ubK15ub deposited by RNF168 (Kitevski-LeBlanc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Kitevski-LeBlanc et al., 2017).

claim: RNF169 is a negative regulator of 53BP1 accumulation at DSBs and promotes BRCA1 recruitment.
source: RNF169 is a negative regulator of 53BP1 accumulation at DSBs and promotes BRCA1 recruitment (An et al., 2018; R. Menon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (An et al., 2018; R. Menon et al., 2019).

claim: 53BP1 binds to H2AK15ub in addition to H4K20me2 which serves as the basis for recruitment of 53BP1 to DSBs.
source: 53BP1 binds to H2AK15ub in addition to H4K20me2 which serves as the basis for recruitment of 53BP1 to DSBs (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Wilson et al., 2016).

claim: 53BP1 binding triggers recruitment and assembly of the 53BP1-RIF1-Shieldin complex where 53BP1 associates with RIF1 which in turn binds to SHLD3, REV7, SHLD2 and SHLD1.
source: 53BP1 binding in turn triggers recruitment and assembly of the 53BP1-RIF1-Shieldin complex where 53BP1 associates with RIF1 which in turn binds to SHLD3, REV7, SHLD2 and SHLD1 (Dev et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Dev et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018) and Figure 1A.

claim: The Shieldin complex directly binds to ssDNA mediated by the OB-fold domains of SHLD2.
source: The Shieldin complex directly binds to ssDNA mediated by the OB-fold domains of SHLD2 (Dev et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Dev et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018).

claim: Resection is carried out by several nucleases including CtIP and the MRN complex, Exo1, and DNA2.
source: Resection is carried out by several nucleases including CtIP and the MRN complex, Exo1, and DNA2 (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: The Shieldin complex promotes end fill-in by recruiting Polα/Primase via the CST (CTC1, STN1, and TEN1) complex through an interaction between SHLD1 and CTC1.
source: In addition, the Shieldin complex promotes end fill-in by recruiting Polα/Primase via the CST (CTC1, STN1, and TEN1) complex through an interaction between SHLD1 and CTC1 (Mirman et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Mirman et al., 2022).

claim: Zeocin is a radiomimetic drug chemically similar to bleomycin that also induces DNA single-strand breaks.
source: To confirm that HaloTagging does not interfere with the recruitment of the tagged proteins to DNA damage sites, we analyzed their sub-cellular distribution by live-cell imaging one hour after inducing DNA DSBs with Zeocin, a radiomimetic drug chemically similar to bleomycin that also induces DNA single-strand breaks (Povirk, 1996; Povirk et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Povirk, 1996; Povirk et al., 1977).

claim: Laser-induced microirradiation (LMI) induces DNA DSBs, but also causes a variety of other types of DNA damage including single-strand breaks and base damage.
source: While laser-induced microirradiation (LMI) induces DNA DSBs, it also causes a variety of other types of DNA damage including single-strand breaks and base damage and likely induces DNA damage at levels typically not encountered by human cells (Holton et al., 2017; Muster et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Holton et al., 2017; Muster et al., 2017).

claim: The PST repeat region of MDC1 was recently reported to associate with the nucleosome acidic patch.
source: For MDC1 we demonstrated that the constitutive chromatin association is mediated by its PST repeat domain which was recently reported to associate with the nucleosome acidic patch (Salguero et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Salguero et al., 2019).

claim: 53BP1 can form phase-separated compartments at DNA lesions.
source: Static 53BP1 molecules within DNA repair foci likely represent molecules directly bound to chromatin while dynamic 53BP1 molecules are likely recruited by the formation of phase-separated 53BP1 compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, Videos 23–24), as observed by others (Kilic et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Kilic et al., 2019) and imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and Videos 23–24.
